newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan 1997 car output seen falling on tax, economy.
newsitem.headline: Japan 1997 car output seen falling on tax, economy.

text.p: After rising for the first time in six years in 1996, output by Japanese carmakers is likely to slip this year, dragged down by a higher sales tax and the poor state of the nation's economy, industry officials said on Monday.

Production in 1997 is projected to exceed 10 million vehicles, but will likely be under 1996's output as exports are not expected to rise and domestic sales will remain flat at best, said an official at the Japan Automobile Manufacturers' Association.
The association announced on Monday that output in 1996 rose 1.5 percent from the previous year to 10,345,786 vehicles, the first yearly output increase in six years.
The rise reflected domestic demand for new recreational vehicles and a recovery in exports late in the year, it said.
But car production in 1997 is likely to slip back to 10.20 million units, Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura said.
"You will see a reaction (in domestic sales) after consumers rush to buy new cars in the first quarter of this year ahead of the planned rise in the consumption tax," he said.
The consumption tax, or sales tax, will be raised to five percent from the current three percent from April 1.
Meanwhile, domestic vehicle sales are likely to remain around seven million vehicles in 1997, given the poor economic outlook and expected after-effects of the consumption tax hike, Sugiura said.
Domestic sales rose 3.1 percent in 1996 to 7.08 million vehicles, the third successive rise on a year-on-year basis.
The industry cannot look forward to much help in 1997 from the weaker yen either, which usually encourages Japan's exports by making them more competitive abroad.
"The weaker yen will not push Japanese carmakers to increase their exports," the association official said.
The association official said Japanese carmakers were unlikely to boost car exports just because of the weaker yen.
On Monday, the dollar stood at just above 119 yen, up about 11 percent from its year-ago level.

"Japan cannot increase its vehicle exports because of trade friction worries. And Japanese carmakers are still boosting their overseas production as planned and they have not revised those plans," the official said.
Japanese carmakers have to be cautious about boosting exports to the United States this year because the earnings of the Big Three there are expected to slip this year, Nomura's Sugiura said.
In addition, Japanese carmakers, except Toyota and Honda, have high inventories in the United States because of poor demand.

The weaker yen is now a mixed blessing for Japanese car makers, as it helps boost foreign exchange income for some, but can also drive up costs, such as for raw materials and for overseas-made components.

"There are concerns that the weaker yen may result in a drop in car imports into Japan and that Japanese car makers may cut their purchases of foreign parts. That will cause a retreat in the reduction of Japan's trade surplus," the car association official said.
